# Long-horizon rearrangement: does an agentic loop survive horizon length and mid-episode disturbance?

*Generated by `python -m harness.report`. Every number below is computed from `episodes.jsonl`; nothing on this page is hand-written, and editing it by hand would be overwritten by the next run.*

## Headline

90 episodes across 2 condition(s) and 9 scene(s). **24** of them ended in a false success — a claimed success the oracle scored as a failure.

| condition | episodes | task success | mean progress | claimed success | honesty gap | false successes | recoveries/ep | escalation rate | mean VLM calls | total tokens | total cost | mean wall s | replay drift |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `one_shot` | 45 | 0.51 (23/45) | 0.74 | 1.00 (45/45) | **+0.49** | 22 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.0 | 135,281 | $0.5644 | 13.0 | 0 |
| `agentic` | 45 | 0.84 (38/45) | 0.91 | 0.89 (40/45) | **+0.04** | 2 | 1.02 | 0.04 | 17.6 | 1,789,336 | $5.0451 | 35.1 | 0 |

honesty gap = claimed success rate minus task success rate, on the same episodes. It is signed: positive means the agent reported work it did not do. `mean progress` is the fraction of graded (block, bowl) conditions satisfied, averaged over episodes: it separates "moved nothing" from "moved three of four", which task success cannot. `replay drift` is the number of cached responses that did not match on replay; anything but 0 means the run is not reproducible.

## One-shot versus agentic: what the loop bought

The two conditions share the model, the tool schema, the pixels, the scenes and the step budget. The only difference is that one plans once and executes blind while the other acts a primitive at a time and reads its own feedback. The delta is the measurement; the absolute rates are context.

| condition | what it adds | task success | Δ task success | honesty gap | Δ honesty gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `one_shot` | blind open-loop: one plan, executed to the end, no feedback read | 0.51 | — (reference) | +0.49 | — (reference) |
| `agentic` | ReAct loop + episode memory + all three verification layers | 0.84 | +0.33 | +0.04 | -0.44 |

Δ is against the row directly above, so the second line prices the loop and nothing else. A negative Δ honesty gap is the improvement: the agent stopped claiming work it had not done.

## Visual verifier error rate

L3 is the only layer that costs money, so it is the only layer that has to justify itself. Here it is marked against ground truth on `disturb_h3`, the scene designed to defeat it.

| quantity | count | rate |
|---|---|---|
| L3 answers on `disturb_h3` | 40 | — |
| answered *yes* (check passed) | 30 | — |
| answered *no* (check objected) | 10 | — |
| **false positives** (said yes, episode failed) | 0 | **0.00** of yes answers |
| **false negatives** (said no, episode succeeded) | 10 | **1.00** of no answers |
| total disagreement with ground truth | 10 | **0.25** of all answers |

computed over the 5 `disturb_h3` episode(s) that actually ran L3, out of 10 on that scene.

The disturbance only fires after the episode's first placement actually lands, so episodes that never placed a block were never disturbed; the effective sample of genuinely perturbed frames is smaller than the episode count these rates are drawn from. `EpisodeResult.disturbed` records which episodes it fired in.

Ground truth here is the **episode** outcome; the harness has no per-step oracle. That makes the false-negative rate an upper bound (an objection the agent then recovered from still counts against the verifier), while the false-positive rate has no such slack. The false-positive number is the one that matters: it is the rate at which the last layer that could have stopped a false success waved one through. It is printed above whatever it says.
